question: What does the study of anatomy primarily focus on?
explanation: Anatomy specifically investigates the physical form and structural relationships of body parts. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why must a nurse study both anatomy and physiology together?

options.A: Hospitals require both subjects for promotion
options.B: It helps in writing long nursing care plans
options.C: Structure dictates how a body part functions
options.D: Physiology is just another name for anatomy

explanation: The physical design of an organ directly determines how it performs its specific role in the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h1)

question: What is the basic living unit of the human body?
explanation: Cells are recognized as the smallest structural and functional units capable of independent life. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h2)

question: An organ is best described as a combination of what lower structural levels?
explanation: Organs are formed when two or more distinct tissue types work together to perform complex functions. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h2)

question: What term describes all the chemical reactions occurring within the body?
explanation: Metabolism encompasses both the breakdown and buildup of chemical compounds in living tissues. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h3)

question: A patient quickly pulls their hand away from a hot stove. Which life process does this show?
explanation: Responsiveness is the ability of an organism to detect and react to changes in its environment. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h3)

question: In the standard anatomical position, where do the palms of the hands face?
explanation: Facing the palms forward is a key part of the universal anatomical position used for medical descriptions. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which body plane cuts the body into upper and lower sections?
explanation: A transverse plane creates a horizontal cross-section, splitting the body into superior and inferior parts. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which muscle separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity?
explanation: The diaphragm is the primary dome-shaped skeletal muscle acting as a physical partition between the chest and abdomen. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of the serous fluid found between membrane layers?

options.A: To reduce friction during organ movement
options.B: To supply oxygen directly to the organs
options.C: To anchor organs tightly to the bone
options.D: To fight off invading bacterial infections

explanation: Serous fluid acts as a lubricant so moving organs like the lungs and heart glide smoothly against cavity walls. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h5)

question: What part of a homeostatic control system detects a stimulus?
explanation: Receptors act as sensors that continuously monitor the internal and external environment for changes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do negative feedback mechanisms protect the human body?

options.A: By speeding up disease progression to finish an infection quickly
options.B: By reversing a directional change back toward a normal set point
options.C: By destroying damaged receptors before they send false signals
options.D: By shutting down all organ systems during times of severe stress

explanation: Negative feedback works to counteract deviations from normal physiological ranges to maintain stability. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T1#GNS111_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which fluid compartment forms the internal environment that surrounds body cells?
explanation: The internal environment consists strictly of the fluid surrounding the cells, known as the extracellular fluid, which includes plasma and interstitial fluid. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why is homeostasis called a dynamic steady state instead of a static condition?

options.A: It requires constant adjustments and energy to maintain internal stability.
options.B: Metabolic processes stop completely when the body is resting.
options.C: Fluids move freely between cells without any physiological regulation.
options.D: Body parameters change drastically throughout every hour of the day.

explanation: Dynamic steady state implies continuous internal activity and regulation to keep values within a normal narrow range despite external changes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h1)

question: In a homeostatic loop, which component compares sensory input against a set point?
explanation: The control center processes incoming signals from receptors and decides what action is needed by comparing the value to the normal set point. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the role of an effector when the body detects a homeostatic imbalance?

options.A: It carries out the final corrective response to alter the variable.
options.B: It transmits electrical impulses directly to the sensory organs.
options.C: It stores excess nutrients until the control center asks for them.
options.D: It detects the initial change in the external environment.

explanation: Effectors such as muscles or glands perform the physical action ordered by the control center to counteract the initial disturbance. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which feedback mechanism works to reverse a change in a regulated body variable?
explanation: Negative feedback loops work to oppose the initial stimulus, bringing the variable back down or up to its normal set point. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT an example of a positive feedback loop?

options.B: Depolarization phase of an action potential
options.D: Formation of a platelet plug in bleeding

explanation: Body temperature regulation relies on negative feedback to cool the body down or warm it up, unlike processes that amplify changes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h3)

question: What term describes an increase in the physical size of individual cells?
explanation: Hypertrophy refers strictly to cellular enlargement due to synthesized proteins and structural components, rather than cell multiplication. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h4)

question: A patient's left ventricle enlarges due to long-standing high blood pressure. What type of cellular adaptation has occurred?
explanation: Cardiac muscle cells cannot easily divide, so they respond to increased workload by increasing in individual size, which is hypertrophy. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h4)

question: What happens during metaplasia in cellular adaptation?

options.A: Complete shrinkage of tissue due to lack of blood supply
options.B: Uncontrolled cancerous growth invading distant body organs
options.C: Replacement of one adult cell type with another adult cell type
options.D: Rapid division of normal cells without any structural change

explanation: Metaplasia is a reversible swap where one stressed cell type is substituted by a hardier cell type better suited to survive that specific irritation. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why is dysplasia considered a clinical warning sign?

options.A: It represents normal physiological recovery after a minor skin scratch.
options.B: It involves disordered growth and nuclear atypia that can progress to cancer.
options.C: It automatically stops the blood supply to the surrounding organs.
options.D: It means the affected tissue has already completely died off.

explanation: Dysplastic cells show abnormal differentiation and organization, serving as a precancerous state that requires close monitoring and intervention. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h5)

question: Which hormone is released by the adrenal cortex during the body's stress response?
explanation: Cortisol is the primary glucocorticoid released during stress to elevate blood glucose and suppress unnecessary energy expenditure. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h6)

question: How does the body react during an immediate sympathetic nervous system response to stress?

options.A: The airways in the lungs constrict to reduce oxygen consumption.
options.B: Digestion speeds up to absorb more nutrients immediately.
options.C: Blood vessels in the skeletal muscles constrict to save energy.
options.D: Heart rate increases and blood is shunted to skeletal muscles.

explanation: The sympathetic response prepares the body for physical action by boosting cardiovascular output and directing blood flow where it is most needed. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h6)

question: How is disease best defined in relation to the body's internal balance?

options.A: A temporary boost in systemic immune function
options.B: An increase in the total number of body cells
options.C: Successful adaptation to an environmental change

explanation: Diseases represent states where the body can no longer keep internal variables within normal physiological limits on its own. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h7)

question: A patient receives intravenous normal saline to treat dehydration. What is the purpose of this nursing intervention?

options.A: It permanently replaces the function of the patient's pancreas.
options.B: It forces the cells to undergo irreversible pathological atrophy.
options.C: It initiates a positive feedback loop to lower blood pressure.
options.D: It acts as an external measure to help restore homeostatic fluid balance.

explanation: When internal regulation fails or is overwhelmed, medical and nursing interventions provide external support to bring the patient back toward stability. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h7)

question: How do the palms face in the standard anatomical position?
explanation: In the standard anatomical position, the palms are turned forward so the thumbs point away from the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is a standard anatomical position necessary for healthcare workers?

options.A: It ensures the patient's blood pressure remains stable during exams.
options.B: It allows doctors to measure height and weight more accurately.
options.C: It is the only comfortable posture for patients undergoing physical therapy.
options.D: It provides a universal reference point to prevent confusion in documentation.

explanation: Using one standard stance ensures everyone describes body locations using the exact same baseline orientation. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h1)

question: A transverse plane divides the body into which two sections?
explanation: The transverse plane cuts horizontally, creating upper and lower portions of the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h2)

question: A CT scan shows a cross-section of the abdomen, dividing it into upper and lower parts. Which plane was used?
explanation: Cross-sections that create upper and lower halves are produced by the transverse plane. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h2)

question: What does the term 'anterior' mean in clinical descriptions?

options.A: Toward the back of the body
options.D: Toward the front of the body

explanation: Anterior describes structures located closer to the front surface of the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h3)

question: The knee is described as being what in relation to the ankle?
explanation: The knee is closer to the attachment point of the trunk than the ankle, making it proximal. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which muscle separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity?
explanation: The diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscular partition between the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which organs are protected inside the dorsal body cavity?
explanation: The dorsal cavity contains the cranial cavity for the brain and the spinal cavity for the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h4)

question: Into how many sections does the quadrant method divide the abdomen?
explanation: The quadrant method splits the abdomen into four distinct areas using intersecting lines at the navel. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h5)

question: A patient complains of sharp pain in the right lower quadrant. Which organ is most likely involved?
explanation: The appendix is typically located in the right lower quadrant, making it a primary suspect in RLQ pain. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary function of body cavities in humans?

options.A: To produce hormones for metabolic regulation
options.B: To protect and support internal organs
options.C: To pump blood throughout the systemic circulation
options.D: To filter waste products from the bloodstream

explanation: Body cavities act as physical spaces that shield delicate internal organs from external trauma and injury. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which two main categories divide the internal spaces of the human body?
explanation: The human body divides its primary internal spaces into the dorsal cavity at the back and the ventral cavity at the front. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which bones form the protective boundary of the cranial cavity?
explanation: The cranial cavity is enclosed by the rigid bones of the skull to protect the brain. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h2)

question: What delicate structure is housed directly inside the spinal cavity?
explanation: The vertebral column surrounds and protects the spinal cord within the spinal cavity. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h2)

question: What muscle separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity?
explanation: The diaphragm is the primary muscle of respiration that physically divides the ventral cavity into upper and lower parts. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h3)

question: What collective term describes the internal organs housed within the ventral cavity?
explanation: Viscera is the anatomical term used for the internal organs located inside the ventral cavity. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the specific name of the cavity that directly surrounds each lung?
explanation: Each lung sits within its own pleural cavity, which provides lubrication and space for respiratory expansion. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h4)

question: Where is the mediastinum located within the chest?
explanation: The mediastinum is the central region of the thoracic cavity situated between the left and right pleural cavities. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h4)

question: Which anatomical structure marks the superior boundary of the abdominopelvic cavity?
explanation: The diaphragm forms the upper roof of the abdominopelvic cavity, separating it from the thoracic cavity. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h5)

question: A patient complains of sharp pain in the right lower abdominal quadrant. Which organ is most likely involved?
explanation: The appendix is typically located in the right lower quadrant, making it the primary organ suspected during localized pain in that area. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the primary function of the fluid found between serous membrane layers?

options.A: To supply oxygen directly to tissue cells
options.B: To reduce friction during organ movement
options.C: To transmit nerve signals to muscles
options.D: To digest food particles in the cavity

explanation: Serous fluid acts as a lubricant, allowing organs like the heart and lungs to glide smoothly against cavity walls. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which layer of a serous membrane is in direct contact with an internal organ?
explanation: The visceral layer covers the surface of the internal organs, whereas the parietal layer lines the cavity wall. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why is an understanding of body cavities essential for accurate nursing documentation?

options.A: It helps communicate precise locations of patient pain and findings
options.B: It determines the exact financial cost of hospital treatment
options.C: It replaces the need for verbal reports during shift change
options.D: It dictates the required visiting hours for family members

explanation: Using standard cavity and quadrant landmarks ensures clear, professional communication among healthcare providers regarding patient assessment findings. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h7)

question: Inflammation of the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity is known clinically as what condition?
explanation: Peritonitis describes inflammation of the peritoneum, which is the serous membrane lining the abdominopelvic cavity and its organs. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T3#GNS111_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of using standard anatomical terminology in clinical practice?

options.A: To replace everyday language during bedside patient conversations
options.B: To prevent confusion during patient documentation and handovers
options.C: To ensure patients understand complex medical diagnoses easily
options.D: To make nursing care plans longer and more detailed

explanation: Standardized terms ensure that healthcare workers across different shifts and locations interpret body locations identically. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h1)

question: A patient is lying flat on their back in bed. Why must nurses still reference the standard anatomical position during assessments?

options.A: It speeds up the process of writing the daily nursing notes
options.B: It prevents pressure ulcers from forming on the posterior surface
options.C: It serves as a universal baseline reference point for body structures
options.D: It proves the patient is resting comfortably without physical distress

explanation: Anatomical position remains the constant point of origin for describing locations, no matter how the patient is positioned. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which part of the body forms the main vertical axis and includes the torso?
explanation: The axial region comprises the head, neck, and trunk, forming the central core of the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h2)

question: The anatomical term used to describe the neck region is:
explanation: Cervical refers specifically to the neck area connecting the head to the trunk. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h2)

question: What structures make up the appendicular region of the human body?
explanation: The appendicular skeleton and regions encompass all the upper and lower extremities attached to the trunk. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h3)

question: A nurse checking a patient's radial pulse is assessing which specific anatomical region?
explanation: The radial pulse is located on the wrist, which is part of the upper limb appendicular region. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h3)

question: How many abdominal quadrants are commonly used for routine clinical documentation and pain assessment?
explanation: The four-quadrant method divides the abdomen into RUQ, LUQ, RLQ, and LLQ for quick clinical reference. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h4)

question: A patient complains of sharp pain in the right lower quadrant. Which organ is most likely involved?
explanation: The appendix is typically located in the right lower quadrant, making pain there a classic sign of appendicitis. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which of the following is an example of an anterior surface landmark on the human body?
explanation: The umbilicus is located on the front (anterior) surface of the abdomen, unlike the scapula and gluteal cleft which are posterior. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why are anatomical surface landmarks particularly important when administering intramuscular injections?

options.A: They ensure the medication is absorbed directly through the skin surface
options.B: They determine the exact chemical composition of the injected drug
options.C: They help identify safe muscle sites and avoid major nerves and vessels
options.D: They eliminate the need to cleanse the skin prior to needle insertion

explanation: Landmarks like the iliac crest or acromion process guide safe needle placement away from vital underlying structures. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why is documenting 'pain in the left calf' clinically superior to writing 'pain in the leg'?

options.A: It provides specific regional detail that guides accurate diagnostic evaluation
options.B: It guarantees the patient will receive pain medication much faster
options.C: It eliminates the requirement to record vital signs during the shift
options.D: It proves the nurse completed a full neurological assessment

explanation: Precise regional terms pinpoint the exact location, helping clinicians rule out conditions like deep vein thrombosis efficiently. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h6)

question: A nurse charting a skin breakdown on a patient's lower back should use which proper anatomical descriptor?
explanation: The sacral region is located on the lower posterior trunk, which is the correct anatomical term for that area. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is recognized as the basic structural and functional unit of life?
explanation: The cell forms the fundamental building block of all living structures and carries out all vital life processes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h1)

question: New cells in the human body are formed by what process according to cell theory?
explanation: Cell theory establishes that biological cells only multiply by dividing from existing living cells. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which structure acts as a selective barrier around the human cell?
explanation: The plasma membrane surrounds the cell, controlling which molecules pass in and out of the cytoplasm. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h2)

question: Where is the primary genetic material of a human somatic cell housed?
explanation: The nucleus stores the cellular DNA, acting as the command center for genetic expression and heredity. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which organelle is primarily responsible for generating ATP energy in the cell?
explanation: Mitochondria act as the powerhouses of the cell, producing chemical energy required for various metabolic functions. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary role of lysosomes within cellular metabolism?
explanation: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that break down cellular waste, damaged organelles, and engulfed pathogens. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h3)

question: What distinguishes active transport from passive transport across the cell membrane?

options.C: Passive transport uses carrier proteins exclusively
options.D: Active transport relies on osmotic pressure

explanation: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, which necessitates the expenditure of ATP. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h4)

question: The movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane is called what?
explanation: Osmosis is the specific term for the passive movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from low solute to high solute concentration. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h4)

question: What type of cell division produces two genetically identical somatic daughter cells?
explanation: Mitosis duplicates somatic cells, ensuring each new cell receives an identical set of chromosomes for tissue growth and repair. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h5)

question: Meiosis is different from mitosis because meiosis results in cells that are...
explanation: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number by half and introduces genetic variation to form reproductive gametes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h5)

question: What happens inside a cell when it experiences severe oxygen shortage (hypoxia)?
explanation: Without sufficient oxygen, mitochondria cannot perform aerobic respiration efficiently, leading to a sharp drop in ATP synthesis. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h6)

question: What happens to body cells when they are placed in a very dilute (hypotonic) fluid environment?
explanation: A hypotonic environment drives water into the cell via osmosis, causing cellular swelling and potential lysis. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h6)

question: What primary developmental period does human embryology cover?

options.A: Throughout the entire duration of childhood growth
options.B: From puberty until the onset of reproductive maturity
options.C: From fertilization up to the end of the eighth week
options.D: From the ninth week until full-term birth

explanation: The embryonic period spans from the zygote stage until the end of the eighth week, after which the fetal period begins. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is studying embryology important for clinical nursing practice?

options.A: It explains the hormonal changes of postpartum recovery
options.B: It provides guidelines for calculating accurate maternal blood pressure
options.C: It teaches nurses how to perform routine surgical deliveries
options.D: It helps nurses understand the origins of congenital anomalies

explanation: Knowing early developmental milestones allows clinicians to trace when and how structural birth defects originate. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h1)

question: How many functional spermatozoa are produced from one primary spermatocyte?
explanation: Meiotic division of a primary spermatocyte yields four equal-sized, viable haploid sperm cells. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h2)

question: At what stage is meiosis arrested in primary oocytes before puberty?
explanation: Primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I from fetal life until specific follicles are recruited during reproductive cycles. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h2)

question: In which anatomical region does human fertilization normally take place?
explanation: The ampulla provides the optimal environment and location where ascending sperm meet the ovulated secondary oocyte. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of the cortical reaction following sperm entry?

options.A: Stimulating the release of luteinizing hormone
options.B: Triggering the rapid shedding of the corona radiata
options.C: Initiating the first mitotic cell division immediately
options.D: Preventing the entry of multiple additional sperm

explanation: The cortical reaction hardens the zona pellucida to block polyspermy, ensuring normal diploid chromosomal integrity. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h3)

question: What name is given to the solid ball of 16 cells formed during early cleavage?
explanation: A morula is the solid clump of blastomeres resembling a mulberry that enters the uterine cavity around the third day. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which part of the blastocyst eventually develops into the embryo proper?
explanation: The inner cell mass gives rise to the tissues of the actual embryo, while the trophoblast forms the placenta. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which hormone produced by the syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum during early pregnancy?
explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) prevents the degeneration of the corpus luteum so progesterone secretion continues. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient asks when the blastocyst typically burrows into the uterine lining. What is the correct response?

options.A: At the end of the fourth gestational month
options.B: Between six and ten days after ovulation
options.D: During the fourteenth day of the menstrual cycle

explanation: Implantation happens roughly a week after fertilization as the blastocyst hatches and attaches to the receptive endometrium. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h5)

question: During which gestational week does gastrulation establish the trilaminar embryonic disc?
explanation: Gastrulation occurs during the third week of development, transforming the bilaminar disc into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which germ layer gives rise to the epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract?
explanation: The endoderm layer develops into the epithelial linings of the digestive and respiratory systems along with internal glands. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h6)

question: What primary structure does the closed neural tube eventually develop into?
explanation: The neural tube is the precursor structure for the entire central nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is NOT a direct result or component of early embryonic neurulation?

options.A: Formation of the definitive skeletal bone marrow
options.B: Thickening of the ectoderm to form a neural plate
options.C: Fusion of neural folds to create a closed tube
options.D: Deepening of the neural groove with raised folds

explanation: Bone marrow formation occurs much later in fetal development from mesodermal tissue, not during early neural tube closure. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h7)

question: At what developmental stage is an embryo most vulnerable to teratogenic structural damage?
explanation: Organogenesis occurs during the embryonic period, making cells extremely susceptible to teratogens causing structural defects. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h8)

question: Why is pre-conceptional folic acid supplementation emphasized for pregnant women?

options.A: It speeds up the process of placental implantation
options.B: It prevents neural tube defects during early closure
options.C: It stops gestational diabetes from developing later
options.D: It cures chromosomal mutations present in gametes

explanation: Adequate folic acid supports proper closure of the neural tube during the earliest weeks of embryonic development. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h8)

question: What nitrogenous base pairs exclusively with adenine in a DNA molecule?
explanation: Adenine always bonds with thymine through hydrogen bonds to maintain the structural stability of the DNA double helix. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h1)

question: The primary role of the genetic code contained within DNA is to direct what cellular process?
explanation: DNA sequences provide the instructions that ribosomes use to build specific proteins necessary for cell function and structure. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h1)

question: How many total chromosomes are found in a normal human somatic cell?
explanation: Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes organized into 23 pairs, inheriting 23 from each parent. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h2)

question: What term describes the alternative forms of a specific gene located at the same locus?
explanation: Alleles are different variations of the same gene that determine distinct traits like eye color or blood type. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h2)

question: What term refers to the observable physical traits of an individual?
explanation: The phenotype represents the physical or biochemical expression of an organism's genetic makeup. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h3)

question: A child inherits a recessive trait. What must be true about their genotype?

options.C: They are heterozygous for the trait
options.D: They carry no alleles for the trait

explanation: Recessive traits are masked by dominant alleles, so an individual must have two identical recessive alleles to show the trait. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h3)

question: Why do males exhibit X-linked recessive disorders more often than females?

options.A: Their immune system is less active
options.C: Their Y chromosome carries mutated genes
options.D: They have only one X chromosome

explanation: Since males have only a single X chromosome, any recessive mutation on it will be expressed because there is no second X chromosome to provide a normal dominant allele. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h4)

question: What pattern of inheritance is demonstrated when AB blood type shows both antigens equally?
explanation: Codominance occurs when two different alleles are both fully expressed in the phenotype without blending. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h4)

question: What is the term for the failure of chromosomes to separate properly during cell division?
explanation: Non-disjunction causes gametes to receive an abnormal number of chromosomes, leading to conditions like trisomy. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which genetic condition is characterized by having an extra chromosome?
explanation: Trisomy means an individual has three chromosomes of a specific type instead of the normal pair. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is the primary genetic cause of Down syndrome?
explanation: Down syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21, resulting from non-disjunction. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h6)

question: A patient with cystic fibrosis primarily struggles with which physiological issue?

options.C: Rapid destruction of red blood cells

explanation: Cystic fibrosis impairs chloride transport, leading to thick, viscous secretions that obstruct the respiratory and digestive tracts. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of constructing a family pedigree in nursing assessment?

options.A: To trace inheritance patterns across generations

explanation: A pedigree chart visualizes family health history, helping clinicians identify genetic risks and inheritance modes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h7)

question: A nurse is caring for a family with a history of a hereditary disorder. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.B: Advise the family to avoid having children

explanation: Taking a family history and drawing a pedigree is the essential first step to assess risk before referring for specialized counseling. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the biological definition of a tissue?

options.A: A group of similar cells working together for a specific job
options.B: A collection of entirely different organs inside a body cavity
options.C: A single specialized cell performing multiple complex tasks alone
options.D: A fluid medium transporting nutrients throughout the circulatory system

explanation: Tissues are formed when cells with similar structures unite to perform a shared function. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h1)

question: Body membranes are primarily composed of which structural elements?

options.A: Rigid mineralized columns supporting the main skeletal frame
options.B: Dense hollow tubes transporting fluid away from the heart
options.C: Thin sheets of tissue covering surfaces and lining cavities
options.D: Isolated floating cells without any fixed structural attachment

explanation: Membranes act as protective or secretory barriers made of tissue sheets across body cavities. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h1)

question: Which primary tissue type is responsible for body movement?
explanation: Contractile cells within muscle tissue enable both voluntary movement and involuntary organ functions. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h2)

question: Epithelial tissue is primarily found doing what in the body?

options.A: Storing excess fat reserves beneath the deep dermis
options.B: Binding skeletal bones tightly together at movable joints
options.C: Transmitting fast electrical impulses down the spinal cord
options.D: Lining body cavities and covering external surfaces

explanation: Epithelia form protective boundary layers on external skin and internal tract surfaces. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which membrane type lines closed internal cavities like the thorax?
explanation: Serous membranes line closed body cavities and secrete watery fluid to reduce friction. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why are synovial membranes classified differently from mucous or serous membranes?

options.A: They open directly to the external environment via hollow tracts
options.B: They cover the entire outer cutaneous surface of the human body
options.C: They lack any lubricating fluid secretion within the joint cavity
options.D: They are composed entirely of connective tissue without any epithelium

explanation: Synovial membranes contain only connective tissue elements unlike epithelial-based membranes. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary difference between regeneration and fibrosis?

options.A: Fibrosis occurs only in skin, while regeneration occurs in bone
options.B: Regeneration requires surgical intervention, while fibrosis heals naturally
options.C: Regeneration restores normal function, while fibrosis creates scar tissue
options.D: Fibrosis replaces cells perfectly, while regeneration leaves fibrous scars

explanation: Regeneration replaces lost cells with identical functional tissue, whereas fibrosis lays down fibrous scar matrix. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why does damage to cardiac muscle tissue often lead to permanent functional deficits?

options.A: Heart muscle cells divide constantly and overwhelm local blood supply
options.B: Fibrous scar tissue prevents blood from flowing through coronary arteries
options.C: Cardiac tissue lacks any connective tissue elements to form scars
options.D: Cardiac muscle has very poor regenerative capacity and heals via fibrosis

explanation: Adult cardiac muscle cells do not divide readily, so healing produces non-contractile scar tissue. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h4)

question: A patient develops a pressure ulcer over the sacrum. Which primary tissue layer is initially compromised?
explanation: Pressure ulcers damage the skin, which is the body's primary cutaneous membrane. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why is adequate nutritional intake essential for a patient with an open surgical wound?

options.A: Vitamins directly destroy bacteria colonizing the deep subcutaneous tissue
options.B: Calories prevent the accumulation of synovial fluid inside joint spaces
options.C: Proteins convert fibrous scar tissue back into functional muscle cells
options.D: Nutrients provide essential building blocks for cellular regeneration and tissue repair

explanation: Cellular proliferation and collagen synthesis during tissue healing require adequate amino acids and vitamins. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T8#GNS111_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the basic structural and functional unit of the human body?
explanation: Cells are recognized universally as the fundamental building blocks that make up all living tissues and structures in the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h1)

question: An organ is best defined as a structure composed of what components?

options.B: Two or more different tissue types working together
options.C: A single uniform layer of specialized epithelial cells
options.D: Independent atoms bonded together by chemical forces

explanation: Organs require a combination of diverse tissues, such as epithelial and muscle tissue, to execute complex physiological duties. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h1)

question: The primary physiological function of the kidneys is to do what?

options.A: Pump oxygenated blood to peripheral skeletal muscles
options.B: Filter metabolic waste and regulate body fluids
options.C: Synthesize digestive enzymes and store excess glucose
options.D: Exchange respiratory gases across alveolar membranes

explanation: Kidneys process blood to clear out toxins and manage fluid and electrolyte balance via urine production. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h2)

question: A patient with severe liver failure will most directly experience impairment in which bodily process?

options.A: Filtration of cellular debris from cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Direct electrical conduction to cardiac muscle fibers
options.D: Exchange of carbon dioxide within the pleural cavity

explanation: The liver is uniquely responsible for metabolizing toxins and manufacturing bile necessary for normal digestion. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h2)

question: Which organ system is primarily responsible for rapid communication and control in the body?
explanation: The nervous system uses electrical signals and neurotransmitters to coordinate immediate responses to internal and external stimuli. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which system works alongside the urinary system to regulate blood pH and fluid balance?
explanation: Blood circulation connects the kidneys and lungs to the rest of the body, allowing continuous monitoring and adjustment of fluid and acid-base balance. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h3)

question: Homeostasis is best defined as what physiological state?

options.A: An unchanging external environment surrounding the human body
options.B: A complete absence of metabolic activity within body tissues
options.C: A stable internal environment maintained despite external changes
options.D: A rapid fluctuation of vital signs during physical exertion

explanation: Homeostasis represents the dynamic equilibrium the body maintains to keep internal conditions compatible with life. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why must multiple organ systems cooperate to maintain normal blood pressure?

options.A: Control relies on rapid neural signals, cardiac output, and fluid volume regulation
options.B: Blood pressure is managed exclusively by hormonal output from the endocrine pancreas
options.C: Skeletal muscles contract continuously to maintain resting vascular resistance
options.D: Digestive organs dictate systemic blood flow distribution during rest

explanation: Blood pressure stability requires the combined efforts of the nervous system for speed, the heart for pumping force, and the kidneys for fluid control. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h4)

question: A patient with impaired kidney function is prescribed a medication cleared through the urinary system. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Switch the medication route from oral to intravenous administration
options.B: Encourage the patient to hold all fluids to rest the kidneys
options.C: Verify renal lab results before administering the ordered dose
options.D: Administer the medication as ordered without checking lab values

explanation: Reduced kidney function delays drug excretion, increasing toxicity risks unless the nurse checks labs and collaborates with the prescriber for dose adjustments. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why should a nurse assess multiple body systems when a patient reports a single localized complaint?

options.A: Organ systems are interdependent, so localized issues often impact other systems
options.B: Localized symptoms never accurately reflect the true source of pathology
options.C: Hospital protocol requires a full head-to-toe assessment for every minor symptom
options.D: Patients frequently exaggerate localized pain to gain attention

explanation: Because body systems rely on each other, a problem in one area quickly triggers compensatory responses or secondary failures elsewhere. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h5)

question: What is the approximate total blood volume in a healthy adult?
explanation: A normal healthy adult human has a circulating blood volume of approximately five liters, depending on body size. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why is blood classified as a connective tissue?

options.A: It forms a rigid structural framework for internal organs
options.B: It connects the skeletal muscles directly to the bones
options.C: It consists of living cells suspended in a non-living fluid matrix
options.D: It contains only solid cellular elements without any liquid

explanation: Blood shares the common embryonic origin and structural setup of connective tissues, featuring cells floating in an extracellular matrix called plasma. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h1)

question: What percentage of whole blood is normally made up of plasma?
explanation: Plasma makes up roughly 55 percent of total blood volume, leaving the remaining 45 percent for formed elements. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h2)

question: What does a patient's hematocrit value actually measure?

options.A: The total amount of dissolved proteins circulating in blood plasma
options.B: The percentage of total blood volume made up of red blood cells
options.C: The exact concentration of electrolytes dissolved in the serum
options.D: The speed at which white blood cells destroy invading bacteria

explanation: Hematocrit represents the proportion of blood volume occupied by red blood cells, which is useful in detecting anemia or dehydration. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which organ is responsible for producing most plasma proteins?
explanation: The liver synthesizes the vast majority of plasma proteins, including albumin, fibrinogen, and most transport globulins. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h3)

question: A patient with severe liver disease develops generalized swelling because of a drop in which plasma protein?
explanation: Albumin is the main plasma protein responsible for maintaining blood oncotic pressure, pulling fluid back into capillaries to prevent tissue swelling. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h3)

question: Why do mature red blood cells lack a nucleus?

options.A: To maximize internal space for carrying oxygen-bound hemoglobin
options.B: To allow them to divide rapidly inside the peripheral bloodstream
options.C: To prevent them from being destroyed by the immune system
options.D: To enable them to produce their own energy through aerobic respiration

explanation: The absence of a nucleus and organelles allows red blood cells to pack in more hemoglobin and adopt a flexible biconcave shape. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which type of white blood cell rises significantly during an acute bacterial infection?
explanation: Neutrophils are phagocytic white blood cells that act as the primary and most abundant responders to acute bacterial infections. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h4)

question: Where does hemopoiesis primarily take place in a healthy adult body?
explanation: Red bone marrow contains the stem cells responsible for generating all circulating blood cells throughout adult life. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary stimulus for the kidneys to release erythropoietin?

options.A: Low oxygen delivery to renal tissues
options.D: High concentration of glucose in plasma

explanation: Hypoxia or low tissue oxygen levels are sensed by the kidneys, triggering them to secrete erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the immediate response of a blood vessel when it is injured?
explanation: Vascular spasm occurs instantly upon injury, causing smooth muscle contraction to immediately minimize blood loss. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the final result of the blood coagulation cascade?

options.A: Dilation of local blood vessels to restore tissue perfusion
options.B: Release of erythropoietin from the renal tubular cells
options.C: Conversion of fibrinogen into a stable fibrin mesh
options.D: Destruction of excess platelets circulating in the plasma

explanation: The coagulation cascade ends with the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, which traps blood cells to form a solid clot. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h6)

question: Which physical sign is most commonly observed in a patient with severe anemia?
explanation: Pallor, or paleness of the skin and mucous membranes, results from reduced hemoglobin levels circulating in superficial blood vessels. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the main danger associated with polycythemia or an abnormally high red blood cell count?

options.A: Increased blood viscosity leading to sluggish flow and clot formation
options.B: Rapid destruction of platelets causing spontaneous internal bleeding
options.C: Inability of white blood cells to fight off bacterial pathogens
options.D: Severe drop in systemic blood pressure due to fluid overload

explanation: An excess of red blood cells thickens the blood, making it harder for the heart to pump and raising the risk of dangerous blood clots. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T1#GNS111_U2_T1_h7)

question: Where do the main coronary arteries originate from?

options.A: The base of the ascending aorta

explanation: Coronary arteries branch directly from the aorta immediately above the aortic valve to supply the myocardium. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why can the heart muscle not use the blood inside its own chambers for oxygen?

options.A: Chamber blood flows too slowly to be useful
options.B: The chamber walls are too thick for diffusion
options.C: Deoxygenated blood fills all four chambers

explanation: Diffusion from the inner chambers cannot reach the thick outer layers of the myocardium, necessitating a separate coronary system. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which specific vessel is commonly known as the widow-maker?
explanation: The left anterior descending artery supplies a massive portion of the left ventricle, making blockages here exceptionally dangerous. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h2)

question: Where does the coronary sinus empty deoxygenated blood?
explanation: The coronary sinus collects venous blood from the heart muscle and dumps it straight into the right atrium for pulmonary circulation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h2)

question: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does most myocardial perfusion happen?
explanation: Muscle relaxation during diastole relieves pressure on the coronary vessels, allowing blood to flow into the myocardium. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h3)

question: A patient develops rapid tachycardia. What effect does this have on their coronary blood flow?

options.A: Perfusion stays the same because vessels auto-adjust
options.B: Perfusion increases because cardiac output is higher
options.C: Perfusion shifts entirely to the systolic phase
options.D: Perfusion decreases due to a shortened diastole

explanation: Fast heart rates cut short the resting diastolic period, reducing the time available for blood to enter the coronary arteries. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h3)

question: What is the approximate resting oxygen extraction rate of the myocardium?
explanation: The heart extracts about three-quarters of available oxygen at rest, leaving minimal reserve for increased demand without raising blood flow. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h4)

question: How do local tissue metabolites regulate coronary vessel diameter during increased exertion?

options.A: They cause vasoconstriction to conserve oxygen
options.B: They block nervous impulses to the heart
options.D: They cause vasodilation to increase blood flow

explanation: Metabolites like adenosine relax smooth muscle in the arterioles, widening the vessel lumen to deliver more oxygenated blood. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the underlying pathological process in the majority of coronary artery disease cases?
explanation: Atherosclerosis involves plaque accumulation inside arterial walls, narrowing the lumen and restricting coronary blood flow. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h5)

question: What distinguishes myocardial ischemia from a myocardial infarction?

options.A: Ischemia is temporary oxygen shortage, while infarction involves tissue death
options.B: Ischemia occurs only at rest, while infarction happens during exercise
options.C: Ischemia causes no symptoms, while infarction causes severe pain
options.D: Ischemia affects veins, while infarction affects arteries

explanation: Ischemia is reversible oxygen deprivation causing angina, whereas prolonged cutoff leads to necrosis, which is a heart attack. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which blood test is considered the most specific biomarker for myocardial cell injury?
explanation: Troponins leak into the bloodstream specifically when heart muscle cells suffer damage, making them the primary diagnostic marker. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a 12-lead ECG during a suspected cardiac event?

options.A: To check serum electrolyte levels affecting heart rhythm
options.B: To measure the exact volume of blood pumped per minute
options.C: To detect electrical abnormalities indicating ischemia or injury
options.D: To visualize physical blockages inside the coronary arteries

explanation: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity, showing distinct waveform shifts when parts of the myocardium are starved of oxygen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is the primary pharmacological action of nitroglycerin in acute chest pain?

options.C: Platelet aggregation to stop clot formation

explanation: Nitroglycerin relaxes vascular smooth muscle, reducing venous return and arterial resistance, which lowers the heart's oxygen demand. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h7)

question: Why is strict bed rest enforced immediately following a femoral percutaneous coronary intervention?

options.A: To keep the patient's heart rate below sixty beats per minute
options.B: To prevent bleeding and hematoma formation at the vascular access site
options.C: To ensure accurate continuous blood pressure readings
options.D: To allow the heart muscle time to regenerate lost cells

explanation: The femoral artery is a large vessel accessed during the procedure, requiring immobility to ensure the puncture site seals properly. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h7)

question: What defines a portal circulatory system?

options.A: A vein connecting two capillary beds
options.C: A direct shunt from vein to artery
options.D: An artery feeding directly into an organ

explanation: A portal system uniquely links one capillary network to another via a connecting vessel before returning to the heart. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why is portal circulation different from normal systemic blood flow?

options.A: It bypasses the heart completely to save energy
options.B: It operates entirely without capillary exchange
options.C: It delivers blood between two capillary networks directly
options.D: It carries only oxygenated blood to abdominal organs

explanation: Unlike standard circulation which goes capillary-vein-heart, portal systems route blood from one capillary bed to a second one before cardiac return. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which two major vessels join to form the hepatic portal vein?

options.B: Inferior vena cava and abdominal aorta
options.C: Gastric vein and inferior mesenteric vein
options.D: Superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein

explanation: The confluence of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein creates the main hepatic portal vein trunk. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h2)

question: What type of blood does the hepatic portal vein primarily carry to the liver?

options.A: Fatty acids absorbed directly into lymph
options.B: Lymph fluid filtered from the kidneys
options.C: Purely oxygenated blood from the lungs

explanation: Blood entering the liver via the portal vein has already passed through GI capillaries, meaning it is low in oxygen but high in absorbed nutrients. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary effect of first-pass metabolism on oral medications?

options.C: Complete conversion into red blood cells

explanation: Liver enzymes break down a portion of ingested drugs before they reach the rest of the body, lowering their systemic availability. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h3)

question: A patient with severe liver disease is prescribed an oral drug with high first-pass clearance. What is the main clinical concern?

options.A: Immediate allergic reaction in the GI tract
options.B: Risk of drug toxicity due to reduced metabolism
options.C: Complete failure of the drug to dissolve in water
options.D: Rapid elimination of the drug through the skin

explanation: When liver function is compromised, first-pass breakdown drops, leading to higher-than-expected drug levels in the blood and potential toxicity. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h3)

question: Which two structures are connected by the hypophysial portal system?
explanation: The hypophysial portal vessels link the base of the brain to the anterior pituitary to deliver releasing hormones. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h4)

question: Why does the body use a portal system for hypothalamic-pituitary communication?

options.A: To deliver releasing hormones directly in high concentrations
options.B: To cool down the brain during high metabolic activity
options.C: To filter out large blood proteins before hormone release
options.D: To mix endocrine secretions directly with digestive enzymes

explanation: Direct vascular linkage prevents hormones from being diluted throughout the entire systemic circulation before reaching the pituitary. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h4)

question: What is the most common underlying cause of portal hypertension?
explanation: Scarring and structural changes in cirrhotic livers obstruct blood flow, raising pressure within the portal vein. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h5)

question: Why do esophageal varices develop in patients with portal hypertension?

options.A: Excess dietary protein creates venous blockages
options.B: Stomach acid erodes the lower esophageal sphincter
options.C: High systemic blood pressure bursts heart valves
options.D: Blood bypasses the blocked liver through collateral vessels

explanation: Elevated portal pressure forces blood into smaller, fragile collateral veins connecting the portal system to the systemic circulation, such as those in the esophagus. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which symptom is a major indicator of hepatic encephalopathy in liver failure patients?

options.A: Severe pain in the right lower quadrant
options.B: Inability to move the lower extremities

explanation: The buildup of neurotoxins like ammonia in the blood due to poor liver filtering leads to confusion and cognitive changes. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h6)

question: A patient with portal hypertension and ascites is admitted to the ward. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Measure daily abdominal girth and track strict fluid balance
options.B: Provide vigorous abdominal massage to relieve fluid pressure
options.C: Encourage a high-protein diet to rebuild liver tissue quickly
options.D: Administer intramuscular injections for pain relief regularly

explanation: Tracking weight and abdominal girth helps monitor fluid retention and the effectiveness of diuretic therapy in ascites. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T11#GNS111_U2_T11_h6)

question: What heart chamber pumps oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation?
explanation: The left ventricle possesses thick muscular walls to generate the high pressure needed to push blood through the entire systemic circuit. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h1)

question: The primary function of the systemic circulation is to supply the body tissues with what substance?
explanation: Systemic arteries carry freshly oxygenated blood and vital nutrients to peripheral cells while picking up metabolic waste products. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which blood vessels are primarily responsible for regulating peripheral resistance and blood pressure?
explanation: Arterioles have muscular walls that constrict or dilate, creating major resistance to blood flow and controlling pressure drops. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h2)

question: What structural feature of capillaries allows for efficient gas and nutrient exchange?

options.A: A single layer of endothelial cells
options.B: Wide lumens to store excess blood

explanation: The extremely thin wall of a capillary shortens the diffusion distance, allowing rapid exchange of gases and dissolved molecules. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h2)

question: What mechanism helps push blood upward through leg veins against the pull of gravity?

options.B: Active pumping by local lymph nodes
options.C: High pressure recoil from the venules

explanation: Contracting skeletal muscles compress adjacent veins, acting as a functional pump that pushes blood toward the heart. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h3)

question: How does a small decrease in the radius of a blood vessel affect vascular resistance?
explanation: Vascular resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius, meaning even minor narrowing causes a sharp rise in resistance. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h3)

question: A patient has cool, pale skin and a capillary refill time of five seconds. What does this finding suggest?

options.D: High cardiac output to the skin

explanation: Delayed capillary refill and cool, pale skin indicate that blood flow to the outer extremities is significantly reduced. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: Checking the strength of pedal pulses is done to assess blood flow through which part of the circulatory system?

options.B: Coronary perfusion to the heart muscle
options.C: Venous drainage from the abdominal organs
options.D: Arterial supply to the lower limbs

explanation: Palpating pulses in the feet tests the patency and pressure of the arterial pathway leading away from the heart into the legs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: Prolonged inadequate systemic perfusion to tissues primarily results in what cellular condition?
explanation: Without steady blood delivery, cells are starved of oxygen, impairing aerobic metabolism and causing cellular injury. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common cause of impaired systemic circulation?

options.A: Arterial vasodilation leading to high volume
options.C: Severe fluid volume deficit or bleeding
options.D: Weakened pumping action of the heart

explanation: Arterial vasodilation actually reduces resistance rather than causing a direct mechanical block or pump failure, though shock can involve maldistribution. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h5)

question: What is the primary fluid transported within the lymphatic system?
explanation: Interstitial fluid that enters the lymphatic capillaries is officially termed lymph. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h1)

question: A major physiological function of the lymphatic system involves absorbing which dietary component?
explanation: Specialized lymphatic capillaries called lacteals in the villi of the small intestine absorb dietary fats. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h1)

question: Which major vessel drains lymph from the lower body and the left side of the upper body?
explanation: The thoracic duct collects lymph from the lower limbs, abdomen, and left thorax, head, and arm. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h2)

question: What mechanism primarily drives the movement of lymph through lymphatic vessels?
explanation: Because there is no heart pump for the lymphatic system, surrounding skeletal muscle contractions squeeze vessels to push lymph forward. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary cellular function of lymph nodes?
explanation: Lymph nodes trap and destroy foreign particles and microorganisms before lymph re-enters the general bloodstream. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h3)

question: Tender and enlarged lymph nodes in a specific body region typically indicate what physiological process?
explanation: Proliferation of lymphocytes and macrophages inside the node during an infection causes temporary swelling and tenderness. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h3)

question: Where do T lymphocytes undergo maturation during childhood?
explanation: The thymus gland secretes hormones that promote the immunocompetence of T cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h4)

question: A patient who has had their spleen surgically removed is most vulnerable to which complication?
explanation: The spleen plays a major role in blood filtration and immune defense, so its absence compromises resistance against encapsulated bacteria. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h4)

question: Which nursing action is important for a patient with arm swelling (lymphedema) after breast surgery?

options.A: Encourage heavy lifting with the arm
options.B: Avoid drawing blood from the affected arm
options.C: Apply hot compresses to the arm
options.D: Keep the affected arm hanging down

explanation: Protecting an at-risk arm from needle pricks and injuries prevents bacteria from entering and worsening the swelling. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the medical term for tissue swelling caused by blocked lymphatic drainage?
explanation: Lymphedema describes the swelling that occurs when protein-rich fluid accumulates in the interstitial tissues due to obstructed lymph vessels. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the primary function of the immune system in the human body?

options.A: Pumping oxygenated blood to body tissues
options.B: Regulating hormonal balance and metabolic rate
options.C: Filtering waste products from the bloodstream
options.D: Protecting the body against foreign pathogens

explanation: The main role of the immune system is to defend the body against harmful invaders like bacteria and viruses. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h1)

question: What happens when the immune system fails to distinguish between self and non-self cells?

options.A: Red blood cells immediately stop carrying oxygen
options.B: Physical barriers like skin become completely dry
options.C: The body develops an autoimmune disorder
options.D: Pathogens multiply without any cellular resistance

explanation: An inability to recognize self-tissues leads the immune system to mistakenly attack healthy body cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which type of immunity is present from birth and acts as a non-specific defense?
explanation: Innate immunity is our inborn, general defense system that reacts the same way to all invaders. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h2)

question: What key feature distinguishes adaptive immunity from innate immunity?

options.B: Absence of any white blood cell involvement
options.D: Reliance solely on intact skin and mucous layers

explanation: Adaptive immunity tailors its response to specific pathogens and remembers them for faster future protection. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h2)

question: Where do T-lymphocytes primarily mature before entering circulation?
explanation: T-cells are produced in the bone marrow but travel to the thymus gland to complete their maturation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h3)

question: What is the primary role of B-lymphocytes in the immune response?

options.B: Acting as the first physical barrier in the skin
options.C: Differentiating into plasma cells to produce antibodies
options.D: Filtering dead red blood cells from the bloodstream

explanation: B-cells transform into plasma factories that secrete specific antibodies to target circulating antigens. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h3)

question: What is an antigen?

options.A: A physical barrier located on the surface of skin
options.B: A protective protein produced by mature plasma cells
options.C: A specialized white blood cell found in lymph nodes
options.D: A foreign substance that triggers an immune response

explanation: Antigens are molecules on pathogens that the body identifies as foreign and reacts against. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h4)

question: Why is the secondary immune response much faster than the primary response?

options.A: Memory cells recognize the familiar antigen immediately
options.B: Antibodies are permanently stored inside red blood cells
options.C: The physical skin barriers are thicker after the first infection
options.D: Pathogens become weaker upon entering the body a second time

explanation: Memory B and T cells left from the first exposure allow the immune system to react instantly. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h4)

question: Which chemical mediator is released during tissue injury to cause vasodilation?
explanation: Mast cells release histamine, which dilates blood vessels and increases permeability at the injury site. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of increased capillary permeability during acute inflammation?

options.A: Cooling down the affected body part to prevent fever
options.B: Stopping blood flow completely to starve out local bacteria
options.C: Preventing red blood cells from escaping the circulation
options.D: Allowing white blood cells to reach the injured tissue

explanation: Permeable capillaries let immune cells and protective proteins exit the blood and enter the damaged area. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of administering a routine vaccination?

options.A: Providing immediate short-term antibodies from donor serum
options.B: Stimulating memory cell production without causing disease
options.C: Destroying all resident bacteria living on the human skin
options.D: Curing an active chronic infection currently in progress

explanation: Vaccines safely train the immune system to recognize pathogens by producing memory cells ahead of real exposure. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h6)

question: What does herd immunity achieve within a population?

options.A: Ensuring that every single citizen receives an annual booster shot
options.B: Eliminating the need for sterile equipment during minor surgeries
options.C: Preventing bacteria from ever mutating inside human hosts
options.D: Protecting vulnerable unvaccinated people through high community immunity

explanation: High vaccination rates in a community reduce disease spread, indirectly shielding those who cannot take vaccines. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h6)

question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction involves immediate IgE-mediated allergic responses?
explanation: Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate allergic reaction driven by IgE antibody binding and mast cell degranulation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h7)

question: What characterizes an autoimmune disease?

options.A: The immune system attacks the body's own healthy tissues
options.B: The body completely lacks any circulating white blood cells
options.C: Pathogens hide inside bone marrow and evade all antibodies
options.D: An allergic reaction occurs only after touching certain metals

explanation: Autoimmunity happens when immune tolerance fails, leading to destructive attacks against self-antigens. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h7)

question: Which nursing intervention is essential when caring for a severely neutropenic patient?

options.A: Implementing strict protective isolation and hand hygiene
options.B: Withholding all prescribed prophylactic antibiotic medications
options.C: Allowing visitors to bring fresh flowers into the hospital room
options.D: Encouraging the consumption of fresh raw fruits and salads

explanation: Protective precautions shield vulnerable patients from acquiring dangerous environmental pathogens. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h8)

question: A patient with low neutrophil counts shows no obvious swelling or pus at a surgical site. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: The suppressed immune system cannot mount a typical inflammatory response
options.B: Bacteria cannot multiply in patients who have low white blood cells
options.C: Antibiotics are actively blocking the formation of local pain receptors
options.D: The surgical wound has healed completely without any cellular help

explanation: Neutropenic patients often fail to display classic signs of infection like pus or marked swelling because they lack white blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h8)

question: Which substance on red blood cells determines an individual's blood group?
explanation: Antigens located on the red blood cell membrane are the specific markers used to classify blood groups. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why do mismatched blood transfusions cause severe immune reactions?

options.A: Recipient red blood cells instantly dissolve
options.B: Hemoglobin turns into a toxic crystal
options.C: Donor plasma attacks recipient white cells
options.D: Donor antigens react with recipient antibodies

explanation: Natural antibodies in the recipient's plasma recognize foreign donor antigens and attack them, causing clumping or agglutination. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: What plasma antibodies are found in a patient with type AB blood?
explanation: Type AB blood contains both A and B antigens, so the body does not produce antibodies against them to prevent attacking its own cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why is type O blood considered the universal red cell donor?

options.A: It stimulates rapid white blood cell production.
options.B: It contains high levels of clotting factors.
options.C: Its plasma lacks all circulating antibodies.
options.D: Its red cells lack A and B antigens.

explanation: Because type O red blood cells carry no A or B antigens, the recipient's antibodies have nothing to attack. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which specific marker determines Rhesus compatibility?
explanation: The D antigen is the most important factor in determining whether blood is Rhesus positive or negative. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: How do Rhesus antibodies develop in an Rh-negative individual?

options.A: Through previous exposure to Rh-positive blood
options.B: Inherited naturally from parents at birth

explanation: Rh antibodies are not naturally present; they develop only after the immune system is exposed to Rh-positive red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of crossmatching blood before a transfusion?

options.A: Detecting adverse reactions between donor cells and recipient serum
options.B: Measuring the exact hemoglobin concentration of the donor bag
options.C: Screening the donated blood for viral infections like HIV
options.D: Determining the precise expiration date of the platelets

explanation: Crossmatching is the final safety check that mixes donor cells with recipient serum to ensure no reaction occurs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: What does reverse blood typing involve in the laboratory?

options.A: Centrifuging whole blood to separate plasma from platelets
options.B: Testing patient serum against known red blood cells
options.C: Mixing patient red cells with commercial anti-D serum
options.D: Heating the blood sample to destroy weak antibodies

explanation: Reverse typing checks the patient's serum against known red cells to confirm which antibodies are present. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which blood group is the universal recipient for packed red blood cells?
explanation: Type AB individuals lack both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in their plasma, so they will not attack incoming red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why is the compatibility rule reversed when transfusing only plasma instead of red blood cells?

options.A: Donated plasma is always filtered to remove cellular debris
options.B: Red blood cells lack the ability to carry clotting factors
options.C: Plasma proteins do not trigger immune responses in humans
options.D: Plasma contains antibodies rather than surface antigens

explanation: Plasma transfusions introduce antibodies into the recipient, so safety depends on ensuring those donor antibodies do not harm the recipient's cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a primary clinical sign of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
explanation: The breakdown of red blood cells releases free hemoglobin into the bloodstream, which passes into the urine and turns it dark. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)

question: When is anti-D immunoglobulin given to an Rh-negative pregnant woman to prevent sensitization?

options.A: Only after the infant is confirmed Rh-negative
options.B: After potential exposure to fetal blood
options.C: During the first trimester of every pregnancy
options.D: Immediately before starting routine iron therapy

explanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin clears any fetal Rh-positive cells before the mother's immune system can produce permanent antibodies against them. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary physiological goal of hemostasis in the body?

options.A: To speed up the overall circulation of red blood cells
options.B: To stop bleeding at injury sites while keeping blood fluid
options.C: To destroy foreign pathogens entering through broken blood vessels
options.D: To transport vital nutrients to damaged tissues during healing

explanation: Hemostasis stops bleeding at injury sites while maintaining normal fluid blood flow throughout the rest of the circulatory system. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h1)

question: Secondary hemostasis differs from primary hemostasis because secondary hemostasis specifically involves...

options.A: immediate constriction of smooth muscle in the vessel wall
options.B: the physical removal of dead tissue surrounding the wound
options.C: the activation of plasma clotting factors to form fibrin
options.D: the rapid adhesion of circulating platelets to exposed collagen

explanation: Secondary hemostasis specifically utilizes plasma proteins called clotting factors to build a strong fibrin meshwork. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h1)

question: What chemical substance acts as a vital bridge for platelet adhesion to exposed collagen?
explanation: Von Willebrand factor acts as the molecular bridge that helps platelets stick to exposed subendothelial collagen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h2)

question: A patient with a deficiency in thromboxane A2 release will most likely experience problems with...

options.A: producing adequate plasma clotting factors in the liver
options.B: recruiting and aggregating additional platelets to form a plug
options.C: initiating the initial vascular smooth muscle contraction spasm
options.D: dissolving the hardened fibrin clot after the tissue heals
